question: On 5 July 2026, the Scarlet Lady, carrying 2 000 LGBTQ+ passengers, was denied entry to the Turkish port of Kuşadası, with local authorities stating that the group’s presence did not ‘align with the structure of our society and our moral values’.

This is part of a broader pattern: Istanbul Pride has been banned every year since 2015, and senior Turkish officials have repeatedly described LGBTQ+ people as a threat to society. The EU maintains active cooperation with Türkiye, and Türkiye remains an EU candidate country.
The promotion of human rights and non-discrimination is a core principle of the EU’s external action under Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union. 1.

Does the Commission, together with the European External Action Service, intend to raise this incident with the Turkish authorities as part of the EU’s political dialogue on human rights, and if so, how?
How is the Commission ensuring that respect for LGBTQ+ rights and nondiscrimination is systematically integrated into the EU’s broader relationship with Türkiye?
What will the Commission do to help protect the rights of LGBTQ+ EU citizens travelling to Türkiye, given the risk of discriminatory treatment such as this?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026)

The European Commission is aware of the denial of entry to the Scarlet Lady in Kuşadası. It has underlined on numerous occasions, including in its last enlargement report on Türkiye1, that the protection of fundamental rights of LGBTIQ+ people in Türkiye remains a major concern. The Commission regularly raises human rights issues with the Turkish authorities.

This includes concerns related to the protection of LGBTIQ+ people’s rights. The Commissioner for Enlargement has met members of the LGBTIQ+ community during her recent visits to Türkiye to discuss the situation.

As an EU candidate country and member of the Council of Europe, Türkiye is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure the respect of fundamental rights for all, including visitors, without discrimination, including on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. These issues are taken into account in the assessment of the country’s alignment with EU values and standards.

The Commission will continue to support civil society and human rights defenders through its financial assistance in Türkiye, including organisations that promote and defend the rights of LGBTIQ+ people.

The Commission will also continue to raise these issues in all relevant contacts with the Turkish authorities, including in the context of the sub-committee covering this area, established under the Association Agreement with Türkiye2.
